notes.b: Physical and cultural regions fade gradually into their neighbours, but governments need clear lines to know who is responsible for what. An administrative region is an area with fixed, legally defined boundaries, set up by a government to organise services, elections and decision-making.
points: Its boundaries are exact lines on a map, unlike the transition zones (gradual border areas where one region shades into the next) of physical and cultural regions.
Governments create administrative regions to deliver services close to people, such as housing, roads and planning (deciding where and what can be built).
They also organise elections fairly, collect statistics and channel funding, including EU regional funds (money the European Union gives to particular regions).
In other words, an administrative region is one involved in governing the functions and organisation of an area.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to match an administrative region to examples: a named county, a county council, a constituency such as Sligo-Leitrim, or a département as an administrative region in France.

notes.b: Administrative regions exist at several scales, from tiny local units up to a union of countries. The list below runs in order from the local scale to the supranational scale.
points: Townland and electoral division: the smallest units (a townland is a very small traditional land area), used for census (the national count of the population) and local purposes.
Local authority area: a county or city council, the body that runs services in that area.
Constituency: an electoral region, the area whose voters elect representatives.
Regional assembly area: a group of counties that plans at regional level, covered below.
The State: the national scale, meaning the whole of the Republic of Ireland.
The European Union: a supranational scale (above the level of individual countries) of 27 member states, since the United Kingdom left in 2020.
notes.tip: A question on how administrative regions operate at different scales is within the syllabus, so be able to go through this hierarchy from smallest to largest with an example at each level.

notes.b: The county is the main traditional unit of Irish administration. Matching questions on administrative regions, set in most years, often use a named county as one of the examples.
points: Counties are the main traditional administrative unit (the unit used to organise local government): 26 in the Republic of Ireland and 32 on the island.
Four provinces: Leinster, Munster, Connacht and Ulster. They are historic and have no administrative function today, so they have no councils and no functions to list.
notes.tip: Do not list council functions for the provinces: they are not administrative regions with councils.

notes.b: A county is not always a single administrative area. Where a county was large or heavily populated, it could be split for administration, and in one case later joined back together.
points: Some counties were divided for administration because of their size or population, which made one council hard to run.
In 1994 County Dublin was divided into Fingal, South Dublin and Dún Laoghaire-Rathdown county councils, alongside Dublin City Council. This is why Dublin has four councils.
North Tipperary and South Tipperary merged in 2014 to form Tipperary County Council, so the county has one council again.
notes.tip: Dublin has four councils, so never say each county has one council.

notes.b: Local councils are the bodies that actually run local services. Their structure was reorganised in 2014, and the old city 'corporations' were renamed.
points: Corporations were the old name for city governments, e.g. Dublin Corporation, which became Dublin City Council in 2002 under the Local Government Act 2001.
Local Government Reform Act 2014: 31 local authorities, made up of 26 county councils, 3 city councils (Dublin, Cork, Galway) and 2 city and county councils (Limerick, Waterford).
The same Act abolished town councils and replaced them with municipal districts (smaller local divisions within a county). There are 949 councillors (elected local representatives) in total.
Councils handle housing, roads and traffic, planning permission and development plans, libraries, the fire service, environment and waste, and parks and amenities.
Councils are funded partly by the Local Property Tax (a yearly tax on homes) and commercial rates (a tax on businesses).
Local elections, which choose the councillors, are held every five years, most recently in 2019 and 2024.
notes.tip: Do not say there are 26 local authorities or that each county has one council. Dublin has four, Cork and Galway each have a city and a county council, and Limerick, Waterford and Tipperary each have one.

notes.b: Administrative boundaries are fixed by law but not permanent. When a city's built-up area spreads past its boundary, the boundary can be moved.
points: Cork City's boundary was extended in 2019 to take in the growing suburbs of Ballincollig, Blarney and Glanmire, and Cork Airport.
There is more on this in the European Regions chapter, which covers growing city regions.

notes.b: Between the county and the State there is a regional level, used mainly to plan regionally and to handle EU money, which is given out by region.
points: Three regional assemblies were set up in 2015: Northern and Western; Southern; and Eastern and Midland. They prepare regional plans and manage EU regional funds.
From 2000 to 2006 Ireland was divided into two regions for EU funding: the Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region and the Southern and Eastern region.
The BMW region held Objective 1 status, the highest level of EU aid, which was given to the regions that most needed support.
There is more on the BMW region's status as a peripheral region (one far from the centre of economic activity) in the notes on Socio-economic regions.

notes.b: A Dáil constituency is an electoral region that elects TDs (members of the Dáil, the lower house of the Irish parliament) by proportional representation (PR-STV, a voting system in which seats are shared out in proportion to votes). It is an electoral region, not a council area.
points: Each constituency elects 3 to 5 TDs.
The Constitution requires roughly equal representation, between one TD for every 20,000 and one for every 30,000 people. Boundaries are therefore redrawn after each census as population shifts.
The Electoral Commission, established in 2023, reviews the boundaries. Before it, constituency commissions did this work.
The 2023 review created 43 constituencies electing 174 TDs, first used in the 2024 general election.
Constituencies often cross county boundaries, because a county's population may not fit a 3-to-5-seat constituency. Sligo-Leitrim is an example.

Growing areas, such as Dublin and its commuter belt (the surrounding towns whose people travel into the city for work), gain seats; declining areas lose them. This shows administrative boundaries changing over time.
Other electoral regions: local electoral areas for council elections, and three European Parliament constituencies in Ireland: Dublin, Midlands-North-West and South.
notes.tip: A constituency's boundaries are not the same as county boundaries. Use only 43 constituencies and 174 TDs; older totals applied to earlier elections and should be left out.

notes.b: For the international setting, the syllabus names the French département. It sits between the commune (the smallest unit of local government) and the region, and exams call it an administrative region in France.
points: Origin: created in 1790 during the French Revolution to replace the old provinces, weaken regional loyalties and centralise power in Paris.
Each was drawn so that every place could reach its main town (chef-lieu) within about a day's ride on horseback, which kept government reachable.
There are 101 départements: 96 in metropolitan France (the mainland and Corsica) and 5 overseas.

Each has a number, originally allocated alphabetically, which forms the first two digits of its postcodes; Paris is 75. Corsica has two départements, numbered 2A and 2B, though its postcodes begin with 20.
Many are named after natural features such as rivers and mountains, e.g. Bouches-du-Rhône (mouths of the Rhône), Haute-Garonne, Seine-Maritime and Pyrénées-Atlantiques.
Government: each has a prefect (préfet), appointed by the national government, and an elected departmental council responsible for social welfare, roads and lower secondary schools (collèges).
notes.tip: Départements are not the same as French regions. Keep 101 départements and 13 metropolitan regions distinct.

notes.b: France has its own hierarchy of administrative scales, and the top tier was reorganised in 2016.
points: France has three tiers of local and regional government: about 35,000 communes, the smallest units, each with a mayor; the départements; and the regions.
In 2016 the number of metropolitan regions was cut from 22 to 13 by merging, to create larger regions able to compete in Europe.
Regions handle economic development, regional transport and upper secondary schools (lycées).
Île-de-France is the region around Paris.
notes.tip: Do not confuse the 101 départements with the 13 metropolitan regions.

notes.b: Setting the two countries side by side shows how much power sits at local and regional level in each.
points: France has three tiers of local and regional government (communes, départements and regions), while Ireland is highly centralised, with weaker local government than France's three tiers allow.

keyTerms.definition: An area with fixed, legally defined boundaries, set up by a government to organise services, elections and decision-making.
A county, city, or city and county council that governs a local area in Ireland.
A sub-area of a local authority that replaced town councils under the Local Government Reform Act 2014.
An electoral region that elects a set number of representatives to a parliament.
Proportional representation by single transferable vote, the system used to elect TDs in Dáil constituencies.
The body established in 2023 to review the boundaries of Dáil constituencies.
A body that prepares regional plans and manages EU regional funds in a region of Ireland.
An administrative region of France, created in 1790, with a prefect and an elected departmental council.
The official appointed by the national government to head a French département.
The smallest unit of local government in France, led by a mayor.
The main town of a French département.

questions.prompt: Explain, with reference to examples you have studied, how administrative regions operate at different scales.
questions.model: Set out the hierarchy of scales, from the townland and electoral division up to the State and the European Union. Irish local authorities: the 2014 reform (31 authorities, municipal districts replacing town councils), the functions of councils and their funding, and the 1994 division of County Dublin as an example of a county divided for administration. Constituencies: PR-STV, 3 to 5 TDs each, the one TD per 20,000 to 30,000 rule, the Electoral Commission and the 2023 review (43 constituencies, 174 TDs), and the cross-county example of Sligo–Leitrim. French départements and regions: origin in 1790 and the chef-lieu idea, the 101 départements and their numbering, prefects and departmental councils, the 2016 reduction of regions from 22 to 13. Compare the three tiers in France with Ireland's more centralised system.

questions.prompt: Explain why constituency boundaries in Ireland change over time.
questions.model: Representation must stay roughly equal, with one TD for every 20,000 to 30,000 people, so boundaries are redrawn as population shifts. Growing areas such as Dublin and its commuter belt gain seats and declining areas lose them. Constituencies are reviewed by the Electoral Commission, and the 2023 review produced 43 constituencies and 174 TDs. Constituencies often cross county lines, as Sligo–Leitrim does, so county boundaries and constituency boundaries do not match.

questions.prompt: Name two levels of local or regional government in France and state one function of each.
questions.model: Départements: social welfare, roads or collèges. Regions: economic development, regional transport or lycées. Communes, each with a mayor and local services, may also be named.
